claims.text: The equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi baseline can be prepared as a stable single-phase FCC alloy.
The investigated quaternary alloys are equiatomic subsets produced by omitting one element from CrMnFeCoNi.
Annealing at 500–700 °C for varied durations followed by rapid quenching can selectively vary SRO while preserving the FCC phase.
The degree of SRO can be quantified using diffuse scattering or related diffraction measurements.
Increasing SRO increases spatial variations in local stacking-fault energy.
Spatially varying stacking-fault energetics modify dislocation mobility.
SRO-induced stacking-fault-energy variations shift the relative activation of twinning and full-dislocation slip.
Enhanced SRO changes the energetic barriers for dislocation nucleation, glide, and twinning.
SRO-mediated changes in dislocation and twinning activity govern differences in yield strength, strain hardening, and ductility.
Increasing SRO will raise yield strength relative to the standard equiatomic quinary baseline.
Increasing SRO will alter strain-hardening behavior relative to the quinary baseline.
Increasing SRO may increase twin density or otherwise modify dislocation arrangements.
Increasing SRO will change ductility relative to the quinary baseline.
Room-temperature in situ TEM of CrMnFeCoNi reveals Shockley-partial activity, stacking-fault formation, trailing-partial glide, and mobile stacking faults.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC high- and medium-entropy alloys without phase separation or precipitate formation.
The mechanism may cease to apply at extreme deformation rates, very high temperatures, or when secondary phases emerge.
Prior evidence indicates that SRO can modestly increase yield strength.
A confirmed change in SRO with no associated change in dislocation behavior, twinning, yield strength, or strain hardening would falsify the proposed mechanistic link.
